title: The Arian question
hookLine: was there a time when the Son was not? A priest's popular songs spread the answer no

cards: Down by the harbor in Alexandria, people are singing theology. Tradition says a priest named Arius put his teaching into catchy verse, and that sailors and millers and travelers picked up the songs and carried them on.
Set to a tune, a hard question goes a long way. Was there a time when the Son of God was not? Arius's songs gave one answer.
His bishop, and a deacon named Athanasius, gave the other. And the argument filled the streets.

teach.h: THERE WAS WHEN HE WAS NOT.
teach.b: First, Arius's side, put fairly. He honored the Son highly. The Son, he taught, was made by the Father before anything else, and through him the world was made.

But made: a creature, the first and greatest, not eternal like the Father. So his followers could say: there was when he was not. It sounded reverent and simple, and it protected the idea that God is one.
Second, the reply. Bishop Alexander, and Athanasius after him, went back to the opening of John's Gospel.

teach.h: IN THE BEGINNING WAS THE WORD.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Not became. Was.
If the Son is a creature, they said, Christians are worshipping a creature.
That was the stake: not a word game, but who Jesus is. Third, the word that decided it.
A council of bishops gathered at Nicaea under Constantine. They wrote a creed, and chose a Greek word for the Son: homoousios, of one substance, one in being with the Father.
The creed said at Sunday Mass grew out of that council and the councils after it.

Fourth, how far the question went. Saint Gregory of Nyssa, writing later about Constantinople, joked about it. Ask a man in the market for change, he wrote, and he gives you a lecture on the begotten and the unbegotten.
Ask the price of bread, and you're told the Father is greater and the Son is less. Ask if the bath is ready, and you hear that the Son was made from nothing.
The question of the age had reached the bakery and the bathhouse.

how: At Sunday Mass Catholics profess the Creed, which says the Son is one in being with the Father, a teaching from the Council of Nicaea that Catholic, Orthodox and other churches share.

games.q: the Arian question — tap the pairs.
p: the Son was made, a creature

s: Arius taught that the Son was just an ordinary man
he called the Son the first and greatest creature, through whom the world was made, but not eternal.
the argument stayed among bishops and scholars
songs, the market and the bathhouse carried it, as Gregory of Nyssa joked.
the council at Nicaea used the word homoousios for the Son
of one substance, one in being with the Father.

games.q: you're a bishop at the council. is the Son made by the Father, or one in being with him? what word goes into the creed?
o: 'homoousios': of one substance with the Father.
leave the question out of the creed.
games.why: the council chose homoousios, and the creed said at Mass today grows from that choice. Arius's teaching was rejected, but the argument went on for years.

practice: In Matthew, after hearing what everyone else says about him, Jesus turns to his disciples: "But whom do you say that I am?"
Let the question sit, without needing the right answer or any answer, and notice what comes up first, and what comes after.
If you pray, bring whatever answer you have, or don't have, to God; if not, let the question keep you company.

wordCard.voice: homoousios. The council of Nicaea's Greek word for the Son, one in substance with the Father, answering Arius's songs. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: of one substance — the council's word for the Son with the Father.

carryVoice: Your line: the question of the age. It's still asked today. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.
